questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Identify a suitable networking device and briefly explain its role in solving the following networking problems.

(i) Linking a LAN to the Internet. (2 marks)

(ii) Linking two large LANs of an institution. (2 marks)

(iii) Controlling the communication signals in and out of an institution's extranet. (2 marks)

(iv) Collecting TV signals from different sources and then channelling them to local TV sets. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Linking a LAN to the Internet: a router (2 marks).** The router connects the LAN to the network of the Internet service provider. It reads the destination address of each data packet and forwards it along the best path towards the Internet, and it passes the packets coming back from the Internet to the right computer of the LAN. (A modem supplies the physical link to the provider's line.)

**(ii) Linking two large LANs: a bridge (2 marks).** The bridge joins the two LANs so that they work as one network. It checks the address of each frame and lets through only the traffic that is meant for the other LAN, so that local traffic stays in its own LAN and congestion is reduced. (A router can also be accepted.)

**(iii) Controlling the signals in and out of the extranet: a firewall (2 marks).** A firewall (hardware or software) examines the data entering and leaving the extranet and allows or blocks it according to security rules. It prevents unauthorised access and keeps out harmful traffic.

**(iv) Collecting TV signals from several sources: a multiplexer (2 marks).** The multiplexer combines the TV signals coming from the different sources into a single channel or cable. At the other end the signals are separated again (demultiplexed) and sent to the local TV sets.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) In each of the following scenarios, identify the Data Transmission Mode and explain how it applies in the given context.

(i) John watching a TV and listening to the commentaries of a football match in his house. (2 marks)

(ii) John and Mary carrying out a conversation using cell phones. (2 marks)

(iii) Paul and Peter sharing information through a walkie talkie. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Simplex mode (2 marks).** Data travels in one direction only: from the TV station to John's TV. John receives the pictures and the commentary but cannot send anything back through the same channel.

**(ii) Full duplex mode (2 marks).** Data travels in both directions at the same time: John and Mary can speak and listen at the same moment, as on a normal phone call.

**(iii) Half duplex mode (2 marks).** Data travels in both directions, but only one way at a time: when Paul presses the button and speaks, Peter can only listen, and then they swap, each saying "over" when he has finished.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) State the reason why technically, 1 kilobyte (KB) = 1024 Bytes ($2^{10}$ bytes) instead of 1 KB = 1000 Bytes. (2 marks)

Hence convert 10 GB to,

(ii) Megabytes (MB) (2 marks)

(iii) Kilobytes (KB) (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Reason (2 marks).** A computer works with the binary system (base 2) and its memory is addressed in powers of 2. $2^{10} = 1024$ is the power of 2 that is closest to 1000, so computer scientists use it as the "kilo" of computing. Hence 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB and 1 GB = 1024 MB.

**(ii) 10 GB in megabytes (2 marks)**

$10\ \text{GB} = 10 \times 1024\ \text{MB} = 10\,240\ \text{MB}$

**(iii) 10 GB in kilobytes (2 marks)**

$10\ \text{GB} = 10 \times 1024\ \text{MB} = 10\,240\ \text{MB}$

$10\,240\ \text{MB} = 10\,240 \times 1024\ \text{KB} = 10\,485\,760\ \text{KB}$
